options: When prices are too high
When economic agents do not have all the information needed to make a rational decision
When a firm has a monopoly
When the government keeps statistics secret
questions.why: Without full information, people struggle to compare options and judge true costs and benefits.

questions.q: Which of these best describes asymmetric information?
options: Both sides of a deal lack information
One party to a deal has more information than the other
Information is expensive to buy
Information is shared equally
questions.why: Asymmetric means uneven: one side knows more than the other.

questions.q: Which is an example of asymmetric information?
options: A car insurer cannot tell how carefully a new customer drives
A shopper forgets to bring a shopping list
Nobody knows who will win an election
A firm has to pay a higher wage
questions.why: The customer knows how they drive and the insurer does not.

questions.q: Imperfect information is a potential source of market failure.
questions.why: If people cannot judge true costs and benefits, they consume too much or too little, so resources are misallocated.

questions.q: People underestimate the long-term benefits of exercise. What is the likely result if this is left to the market?
options: Too much exercise
Too little exercise
The right amount, as prices adjust
No change in behaviour at all
questions.why: If the benefit is underestimated, people take too little of it compared with what would be best for them.

questions.q: Which of these would most directly reduce asymmetric information in the used car market?
options: A subsidy for new cars
A legal requirement to show a car's full service and accident history
A higher tax on fuel
A rise in interest rates
questions.why: Making the history available gives buyers the information the seller already has.

questions.q: Explain why asymmetric information can cause buyers of second-hand cars to be worse off.

ideas.label: The seller knows more about the car's faults or quality than the buyer
So the buyer may pay too much for a bad car, or avoid buying at all

questions.model: The seller knows more about the car's quality and faults than the buyer. The buyer cannot tell a good car from a bad one, so they may pay too much for a faulty car, or avoid buying at all and miss out on a good one.
questions.why: Uneven knowledge means the buyer can pay more than the car is worth to them.

tests.answer: The seller knows more about the faults, so the buyer may pay too much for a bad car.
The seller has more information than the buyer.
